t: An Alabama defense lawyer drops his appeal of a $5,000 sanction for AI-generated fake citations in a drug conspiracy case
d: A federal appeals court dismissed the appeal after the lawyer said the 12 months of required disclosures had already run, FOX10 News reports.

t: Prosecutors object as the defense in a former OpenAI engineer's eavesdropping case plans to review evidence with Anthropic's Claude
d: A federal judge said he was "a lot less concerned" than prosecutors and asked them to put the objection in a written motion, Quartz reports, citing CNBC.

t: Wisconsin Supreme Court dismisses a petition asking for statewide rules on generative AI in court proceedings
d: The Nov. 16 order cites procedural shortcomings with the petition and says the court will not further consider it.

t: Harris County Sheriff's Office limits Flock plate-reader searches to higher-ranking officers and active criminal investigations
d: The new policy takes effect immediately, months after three deputies had their Flock access suspended for possible misuse, ABC13 reports.

t: Poughkeepsie's Common Council overrides the mayor's veto, and the city's Flock cameras are being removed
d: Seven members voted to override Mayor Yvonne Flowers, who says the council acted without public hearings; police say the cameras were disabled Nov. 18, Mid Hudson News reports.

t: Harris County pulls a proposed Clearview AI facial recognition contract from its commissioners' agenda
d: The sheriff's office said the agreement was not ready for consideration and would not say whether it will return.

t: Richland, Washington, approves a $922,861.65 Axon purchase to expand its police drone-as-first-responder program
d: The five-year order covers added equipment, software, licensing and related services, paid with previously approved state grant funds.

t: Pinehurst, North Carolina, approves a free one-year police drone trial that rolls into five paid years unless it gives notice
d: Motorola's paperwork lists five paid years at $159,998 each after the free year, a $799,990 total, DroneXL reports from the council packet.

t: ICE is paying AT&T for access to raw phone data and analysts who search it, 404 Media reports
d: An internal ICE procurement document says the arrangement gives the agency "access to AT&T's raw data and experienced analysts." Experts call it a mass surveillance program.

t: ICE moves to keep nationwide license plate reader access with a $1.2 million sole-source bridge contract
d: A November 12 federal notice names Thomson Reuters Special Services for a four-month deal; the current agreement expires November 30.

t: Fountain Hills, Arizona, permanently bans license plate readers and buying their data in a 5-2 vote
d: The ordinance covers Flock cameras and any similar vehicle identification technology, plus plate-reader data and search services.

t: Suffolk County sheriff's office says it shares Flock plate data with more than 400 agencies without written agreements
d: Officials told Southold's Town Board the sharing is set through Flock's settings; they could not answer some questions about data security and encryption.

t: Quincy's mayor rejects the council's power to approve new police surveillance tech but keeps the rest of its ordinance
d: The council passed the surveillance ordinance 8-1; Mayor Thomas Koch struck one sentence requiring a council vote before the city acquires covered technology, calling it beyond the scope of the council's authority.

t: Chicago City Council orders an audit of every city vendor that provides license plate readers
d: The order, passed 42 to 8, directs the Office of Public Safety Administration to check that vendors are not violating privacy laws or the state law that bars information sharing with federal immigration enforcement.

t: Little Rock weighs an ordinance adding oversight rules for police surveillance technology after a plate reader misuse audit
d: The proposal covers license plate readers, facial recognition, gunshot detection, drones and cameras with automated analytical capabilities; a third and final reading is set for Dec. 1.

t: South Korea's justice ministry plans to pilot an AI system in 2027 that warns of reoffending risk among people on electronic monitoring
d: The system would analyze location data, crime information and interview records of sex offenders under electronic monitoring; officers already carry about 20 cases each, the ministry says.

t: An Arizona court commissioner drops a felony charge at a first appearance and says AI drafting limits the weight of a Gilbert police report
d: It is the second case in a couple of weeks in which the same Maricopa County judicial officer has questioned a probable cause statement written with Axon Draft One, AZFamily reports.

t: Chile's prison service tests an AI data system to help decide who moves to its education-and-work reintegration centres
d: Gendarmería's Biobío project, in its second round of testing with real data, aims to fill unused places in the Centros de Educación y Trabajo, G5noticias reports.

t: Kenya's Judiciary pilots Mahakama AI, an in-house research tool for judges, as it faces nearly 580,000 pending cases
d: The courts say they are finalising an AI policy that would bar judicial officers from putting confidential case data into unapproved systems, The Star reports.

t: New York bill would make judges who knowingly or recklessly cite AI-fabricated law guilty of misconduct
d: State Sen. Michelle Hinchey's Judicial AI Accountability and Integrity Act would let the judicial conduct commission refer cases to the Assembly for impeachment; she will push it in 2027.

t: China's Supreme People's Court consults on draft rules for AI-assisted trials after piloting its own large model in some courts
d: Court leaders say judges must stay in charge and efficiency must never be pursued one-sidedly, according to the court's news service.

t: India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands write biometric ID, CCTV and linked digital records into a new prison law
d: The regulation, published November 18, 2026, repeals the Prisons Act, 1894, and also sorts inmates by security risk.

t: Cass County approves a $9.6 million Axon contract that adds Draft One AI report writing for sheriff's deputies
d: Deputies and supervisors must review and approve every AI-drafted report, and the sheriff says officers who lie about reviewing one will be fired.

t: Knoxville police start sending drones to 911 calls from 12 docks across the city
d: The department says its policy limits flights to emergency calls and bars random patrols, with audits and a public transparency dashboard.

t: New Orleans police launch drones as first responders in the French Quarter
d: NOPD soft-launched the program on Oct. 23 with four drones; the City Council now requires a report on the department's drone program.

t: London Assembly opens an investigation into how the Met uses AI in frontline policing
d: The Police and Crime Committee will examine the AI tools in use, being tested or planned, and how the Mayor's policing office oversees them.

t: Hertfordshire police take live facial recognition to three town centres during a national knife crime week
d: The force lists Watford High Street for Saturday, 21 November 2026, after earlier stops this week; its own table shows 1 alert across past deployments that report results.

t: Arizona police ran more than 110,000 searches of Flock's plate-reader database without paid contracts, AZCIR finds
d: At least eight agencies, including Phoenix police, got access through no-cost deals with the company or through other agencies.

t: Colorado judge lets a class action over Boulder police's Flock cameras proceed and rejects a contract-based records denial
d: The judge said a contract with Flock does not let the city evade its duties under the state's criminal justice records law.

t: Plaintiffs appeal the dismissal of their lawsuit over San Jose police's warrantless searches of Flock camera data
d: The suit by SIREN and CAIR-CA, represented by EFF and the ACLU of Northern California, targets searches of nearly 500 cameras.

t: San Diego City Council rescinds police use policies for license plate readers and Smart Streetlights; the mayor says he will not veto
d: The council kept 52 other surveillance use policies in its annual TRUST Ordinance review. A payment of about 2 million dollars tied to the contract was due in December.

t: A federal advisory agency asks the public how judges and parties in agency hearings should be allowed to use generative AI
d: The Administrative Conference of the United States will use the comments to recommend best practices for federal agencies. Comments are due January 19, 2027.

t: Fairfax County cuts plate-reader data retention to seven days and limits access to about 50 officers
d: The chairman's Board Matter, which the Board of Supervisors backed, also bars most data sharing with other agencies and directs a move away from Flock Safety.

t: Santa Ana City Council votes unanimously to end its Flock and Motorola plate-reader agreements
d: The council also asked staff to look into the legality of banning such cameras on private property.

t: Immigrant rights groups ask a federal judge in Charlotte to make ICE publish its full memo expanding GPS ankle monitoring
d: The government says a copy that surfaced in a Pennsylvania court case makes the lawsuit moot. The judge asked both sides for written arguments.

t: UK justice ministry pilots a tool that gives probation staff faster access to GPS tag data in three regions of England
d: The ministry says staff have run over 30,000 searches and that it aims to reach all probation regions by the end of 2026. The figures are its own.

t: Michigan's prison agency and its contractor say the new prisoner classification software is not AI; two of three experts question that
d: The system, to be piloted starting Dec. 1, uses a points formula built from 10 years of state data. One professor told the Detroit Free Press it is "definitely an automated decision system" and a form of AI.

t: Clark County, Nevada, approves a $3,900,000 federal grant proposal for an AI supported intelligence platform at its detention center
d: County commissioners passed the item on Nov. 3, 2026. The county record describes a platform to analyze data for contraband mitigation, crime reduction and investigations. It is an application, not an award, and no vendor is named.

t: El Dorado County, California, renews biometric monitors for people in its jails as questions remain about whether they can refuse them
d: Supervisors voted 5-0 on Nov. 17 to keep the 4Sight Labs devices, which track location and vital signs, the Sacramento Bee reports. The sheriff's public policy manual does not address the system.

t: A Florida sheriff's office will replace its jail body scanner with one that uses AI to help detect contraband, paid for by a state grant
d: The Flagler County Sheriff's Office says the scanner is part of $2.4 million in state grant funding announced Nov. 16, 2026. The release names no vendor and gives no detail on how the AI works.

t: Pakistan's Sindh province inaugurates an AI-based CCTV and command and control system at Malir Jail and plans it for all its prisons
d: The Inspector General of Prisons said the system will keep records of visitors, The News reported on Nov. 19, 2026. No vendor, cost or data rules were reported.

t: UK justice ministry publishes how its reoffending-risk tools work: scores used in pre-sentence and parole reports come from models trained on a 2018 caseload
d: A new government transparency record describes five tools that prison and probation staff calculate daily, and says the models have no fixed retraining schedule.

t: Colorado gives parole officers an optional AI tool that drafts their meeting notes; the state says it makes no supervision decisions
d: The corrections department says officers had used the Recidiviz tool to document more than 800 meetings by Nov. 4 and must approve every draft note.

t: A reentry nonprofit says its AI phone coach for job interviews raised placements in an internal pilot, and it is holding back a parole-hearing version
d: The Center for Employment Opportunities' chief executive describes the tools in a Vital City essay; the figures are the organization's own.

t: Tulane researchers turn New Orleans court dockets into trackable case histories and find detained defendants plead guilty more often
d: A preprint describes software that reads clerk notes from 130,640 cases; the authors say the patterns need more context before conclusions are drawn.

t: London's Met Police starts a six-month pilot of handheld facial recognition on the street and in custody suites
d: One hundred officers can check a photo against the force's custody images; the UK biometrics commissioner says national oversight plans still lack detail.

t: Nottinghamshire Police report nine arrests from a facial recognition van, including two men wanted on recall to prison
d: The force also says officers stopped people who were not on the watchlist because they avoided the vehicle.

t: Hong Kong begins switching on facial recognition across its police CCTV network, with 60,000 camera points planned by 2028
d: Police say access needs prior authorisation and is logged; the system's stated purposes include national security.

t: A police-partnered program shows AI-generated moving images of Canada's 25 most wanted and won't say how they were made
d: Privacy and criminology experts told CBC there is no way to check the likenesses or count false leads.

t: A federal evidence rule for AI-generated material is back in revision and unlikely to take effect before late 2028, an ABA update says
d: Until then, judges are testing AI evidence under the existing expert-reliability rule.

t: Study: language models reading parole hearing transcripts predicted rearrest about as well as a statistical tool, but their stated reasons didn't match
d: The lead researcher says the results do not mean such models are ready to make parole decisions.

t: Idaho Supreme Court releases a report on when and how state courts may use AI; it adopts no tool
d: A workgroup of judges, lawyers and court staff proposes a standing committee to advise the court on AI.

t: Utah prosecutors drop their plan to play an AI clone of a murdered woman's voice at a death penalty re-sentencing
d: Weber County told the judge on Nov. 20 that the AI company refused a license and no other voice-cloning provider would work with it, KSL reports. The judge had not ruled on whether the clone could be used.

t: Justice Department ethics office finds two of its attorneys broke conduct rules in using AI and refers both for review
d: One assistant U.S. attorney filed a pleading with fabricated quotations and then misled the court about it. Another attorney uploaded documents covered by a protective order to a public AI platform.

t: Around 25 judges are testing AI chatbots in their chambers through a Penn law school pilot, the Inquirer reports
d: Judges in the federal court in Philadelphia use the tools to schedule hearings and draft jury instructions. The professor who runs the program says the tools are "pretty bad at legal research."

t: Stanford researchers find signs of AI drafting in more than a third of the Santa Clara court complaints they examined
d: Among self-represented filers in Santa Clara, the share went from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. The researchers warn that detectors can estimate how common AI use is, but cannot reliably pinpoint which filings used it.

t: European Court of Human Rights bars a Romanian lawyer for two years over unverified AI-generated citations
d: The court says her filing cited non-existent cases and fictitious paragraphs in real judgments. She acknowledged using AI tools to draft it.

t: New York's NYPD watchdog finds the department broke its own facial recognition policy in some cases and issues 17 recommendations
d: The Department of Investigation's inspector general says the NYPD largely complies with the POST Act, but one internal log showed about a third of face searches marked "no" for supervisor review.

t: New York bill would make it judicial misconduct to put fabricated legal authority in a ruling
d: State Sen. Michelle Hinchey's bill says using AI alone is not misconduct, but knowingly or recklessly including made-up citations would be, Reuters reports.

t: An OpenAI Foundation grant will add an AI literacy course to a job program inside three Indiana women's prisons
d: The Televerde Foundation received $200,000 to build the course and an AI-powered resource center for graduates of its PATHS reentry program, Free Press Indiana reports.

t: Michigan will pilot a new scoring system for prison security levels on Dec. 1, and its developer says AI plays no part in the score
d: The Michigan Department of Corrections says the redesigned classification system, built with the nonprofit Recidiviz, should predict future violence about 30% better. It has not said how it reached that figure.

t: Two US judges refuse to let AI output stand in for probable cause, as Fargo defends a $10 million false-arrest suit
d: An Arizona judge released a DUI suspect because an AI tool helped write the arrest report. A Kentucky federal judge let a wrongful-arrest suit over a face match proceed. Fargo says its officers broke no law.

t: UK inspection finds police can't show how much retrospective facial recognition helps
d: From the archive (Nov 12, 2026): Forces make more than 300,000 search requests a year; the report sets 16 recommendations.

t: Japan puts AI translation devices in 129 detention facilities so staff and foreign inmates can talk
d: From the archive (Nov 10, 2026): The Ministry of Justice handed out about 200 palm-sized translators. Only 28 interpreters serve the whole system.

t: More UK forces roll out live facial recognition as Hampshire reports 406,001 faces scanned in a year
d: From the archive (Oct 30, 2026): Suffolk planned deployments in three towns with equipment borrowed from Bedfordshire Police.

t: France will run riot suspects' social media images through its criminal records face database
d: From the archive (Oct 23, 2026): Facial-recognition lookups in the TAJ database rose from about 375,000 in 2019 to about one million in 2024.

t: 35 House Democrats ask ICE how it reaches Flock's plate-reader network through local police
d: From the archive (Oct 23, 2026): The letter set a Nov. 20 deadline for answers on legal authority and policy.

t: Mill Valley, California, suspends its Flock cameras after the company changes its terms of use mid-contract
d: From the archive (Oct 23, 2026): The city says the new terms lacked enforceable privacy protections; the cameras have been off since Sept. 9.

t: Law Commission of Ontario issues 29 recommendations on AI in criminal justice
d: From the archive (Oct 22, 2026): They include provincial legislation, risk assessments for police AI and resources for accused people to respond when AI is used.

t: Poll: most voters want plate-reader cameras limited or restricted
d: From the archive (Oct 22, 2026): 39% say use them only for serious crimes or emergencies; 25% say they pose too much privacy risk.

t: UK Home Office publishes its data protection assessment for live facial recognition
d: From the archive (Oct 22, 2026): The 62-page document covers the software, hardware and deployment processing.

t: Bayfield County, Wisconsin, committee withdraws its call for a countywide Flock camera policy
d: From the archive (Oct 22, 2026): The county will first gather its existing surveillance policies; the sheriff runs six plate readers.

t: In Duplin County, North Carolina, one town awaits Flock cameras while the sheriff's office decides against them
d: From the archive (Oct 22, 2026): Wallace's police chief defended the readers; the sheriff's office cited the controversy.

t: Alexandria police still haven't decided who will review their plate-reader audits
d: From the archive (Oct 21, 2026): The city's Independent Policing Auditor post has been vacant since Oct. 3.

t: Fairfax County supervisors spend two hours on the future of 84 Flock plate readers and reach no decision
d: From the archive (Oct 21, 2026): Police cited 938 arrests since 2022; several supervisors said privacy questions went unanswered.

t: Analysis: DHS's AI inventory labels few ICE and CBP tools high-impact, leaving safeguards unclear
d: From the archive (Oct 21, 2026): Two Brennan Center authors say the federal inventory law isn't delivering transparency.

t: Sterling Heights, Michigan, renews its Flock contract and moves usage reviews to every 30 days
d: From the archive (Oct 21, 2026): A councilman who voted no wanted to make officer misuse of the data a local misdemeanor.

t: Springfield, Illinois, renews ShotSpotter for $1.1 million as a request for more data fails 5-4
d: From the archive (Oct 21, 2026): An alderman wanted information on false alarms and sensor placement before the three-year purchase.

t: San Diego council committee votes unanimously to switch off the city's plate readers; the mayor opposes it
d: From the archive (Oct 21, 2026): The full council still has to vote, and the mayor could veto.

t: Clearview AI takes its fight over a UK privacy fine to the Court of Appeal
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): The facial recognition firm challenges a penalty of more than £7.5 million; no judgment date is set.

t: Waukegan police officer charged with using plate readers to track co-workers' cars
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): He faces five felony counts of official misconduct; a department-wide database audit is underway.

t: Indiana prosecutor threatens to sue county leaders who want to cover Flock cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): The county council voted not to fund the contract; commissioners want to bag the six plate readers.

t: Appeal argues Flock camera tracking without a warrant should void a 60-year sentence
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): A Texas man convicted of five armed robberies says police needed a warrant to build a 'pattern of life' from plate data.

t: Delhi Police seek 338 facial recognition cameras as a rights group questions AI-equipped riot vans
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): The Internet Freedom Foundation says the vans' paperwork doesn't say what the cameras record.

t: Stanford replaces its Flock plate readers with Genetec cameras; faculty critics say the approach hasn't changed
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): Installation was about half done and the 30-day retention period stays the same.

t: Henrico County and Richmond, Virginia, move to cancel Flock contracts as a study finds cameras clustered in Black neighborhoods
d: From the archive (Oct 20, 2026): The Appeal reports on the cancellations and a Hampton Roads camera-placement study.

t: Georgia arrests a former police sergeant for misusing a Flock license plate reader system
d: From the archive (Oct 19, 2026): An internal audit at the Vidalia Police Department led to two counts of misuse of a license plate reader system.

t: West Virginia House Republicans ask Flock to testify under oath after calling its written answers incomplete
d: From the archive (Oct 19, 2026): Four committee members set a Nov. 9 hearing and had earlier threatened subpoenas.

t: Jackson, Mississippi, police will not renew the city's contract for 16 Flock cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 19, 2026): A council member says the council was not told the specific reason.

t: Wausau, Wisconsin, committee schedules closed-door legal advice on ending its $250,000 Flock contract
d: From the archive (Oct 18, 2026): The city pays $50,000 a year for 20 cameras; officials disagree on whether a contract clause lets it stop paying.

t: Vallejo oversight panels question whether audits of about 5,000 plate-reader searches a quarter are big enough
d: From the archive (Oct 16, 2026): Police check 30 random Flock searches at a time. Commissioners wanted a larger sample; the department cited staffing.

t: Sun Prairie, Wisconsin, police propose moving plate readers from Flock to Axon as residents object
d: From the archive (Oct 16, 2026): The chief offered a 14-day data retention trial; opponents said a new vendor doesn't answer their concerns.

t: GAO: ICE can't tell whether officers turn on body cameras; DHS rejects automatic activation
d: From the archive (Oct 15, 2026): DHS agreed with six of seven GAO recommendations. ICE had issued no reprimands for camera-policy violations.

t: Indian police load 850 people's photos into facial recognition at a temple festival
d: From the archive (Oct 14, 2026): Kolhapur police say thefts dropped; the report notes an alert alone doesn't show anyone committed a crime.

t: Malaysia weighs China-style facial recognition cameras at crime hotspots
d: From the archive (Oct 14, 2026): Deputy Prime Minister Zahid cited a Johor pilot but said budget limits could block a national rollout.

t: Police memos show agencies treating AI as both a terror tool and a target
d: From the archive (Oct 14, 2026): The Guardian reviewed 80+ law enforcement documents; they also show monitoring of online opposition to data centers.

t: ACLU of Wisconsin and EFF ask the state Supreme Court to require warrants for searches of plate-reader data
d: From the archive (Oct 14, 2026): The petition names four cities and was filed for a church council and a pastor.

t: Texas comptroller bars state grant money for license plate readers; local and federal funds are still allowed
d: From the archive (Oct 14, 2026): The ban covers all future grants administered by the comptroller's office.

t: San Diego police explore AI to help officers write reports, a contract estimated at up to $3 million
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): The department calls it an exploration phase; it barred non-approved AI report tools in December.

t: ICE buys AI social media listening tools in a contract worth just under $1 million
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): The vendor says the tools can't be used for facial recognition; the record doesn't show how ICE will use them.

t: UK names a permanent director for its £75m national police AI centre
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): Projects include exploring AI to prepare and quality-check evidence case files.

t: UK Home Office sets rules for live facial recognition in immigration enforcement, including transport hubs
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): Non-alert images are to be automatically and permanently deleted, Biometric Update reports.

t: San Diego councilmember who backed the city's 500-plus Flock cameras now wants the contract canceled
d: From the archive (Oct 15, 2026): The police chief and mayor still support the network, which faces an ACLU lawsuit.

t: The Ban Flock Act, H.R. 10691, would bar federal agencies from plate-reader systems, including ones on drones, without congressional authorization
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): The bill would also tie aid from five federal departments to state and local limits.

t: Manvel, Texas, cancels its Flock contract and covers all 16 cameras within 48 hours
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): In nearby Pearland, about 63% of searches over a year came from out-of-state agencies, a crime analyst said.

t: San Diego Councilmember Stephen Whitburn, a past supporter, calls for the city to turn off its Flock cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): The police chief said the technology has helped solve more than 900 cases.

t: Penn State ends its Flock license plate reader pilot and removes the cameras from its main campus
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): A senior vice president cited cost, return on investment and operational value.

t: Virginia's Nelson County sheriff ends Flock plate-reader use, citing privacy and possible misuse by his own office
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): The sheriff said the three cameras had been effective but ended the contract anyway.

t: Inkster, Michigan, signs a 10-year Flock expansion with 20 plate readers, 48 gunshot sensors and a drone
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): The city started with six readers in 2023; the drone was due to go live by early December.

t: Kennesaw State students protest about 49 Flock cameras on their two Georgia campuses
d: From the archive (Oct 13, 2026): A student group estimates the university spent $400,000 on Flock devices; the university did not comment.

t: Madison Heights, Michigan, disconnects its city-run Flock cameras and will let the contract lapse
d: From the archive (Oct 11, 2026): Officials say Flock couldn't provide the safeguard assurances the city wanted.

t: New York's Capital Region splits over plate readers bought with state grants; one county's supervisors say they weren't told
d: From the archive (Oct 11, 2026): Columbia County's sheriff spent $97,129.58 of a state grant on 10 cameras, the Daily Gazette reports.

t: ICE records show agents took in 50.6 million voter records and examined more than 120 nonprofits
d: From the archive (Oct 9, 2026): Records obtained through FOIA don't show the voter data entered Palantir's ELITE system; Palantir says it never did.

t: Spain's data regulator tells two towns to add safeguards before AI video surveillance
d: From the archive (Oct 9, 2026): One project has facial recognition features; the other adds 38 cameras with AI person search.

t: ICE asks vendors about one AI system to analyze detainee calls, messages, video visits and cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 9, 2026): The request describes voice profiles built from recorded calls, including checks on who answers.

t: Lakeland, Florida, approves a nearly $22 million Axon contract that includes Draft One AI report writing
d: From the archive (Oct 9, 2026): Florida does not require police to disclose which reports were drafted with AI, WMNF notes.

t: Suffolk County lawmakers question Flock representatives and say they will look at plate-reader guardrails
d: From the archive (Oct 8, 2026): A nearly $4 million gunshot detection contract with the company has been delayed, Newsday reports.

t: Seven Berkeley council candidates pledge to remove the city's 52 plate-reader cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 7, 2026): They urged the council to delay a vote on a new surveillance contractor.

t: Colorado's Custer County Sheriff's Office ends its Flock plate-reader contract and removes the cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 7, 2026): The office says it doesn't plan to install another plate-reader system.

t: Congress gets competing plate-reader bills: a funding ban from Sanders, audit and deletion rules from Hawley
d: From the archive (Oct 6, 2026): A third, Republican House bill has drawn six GOP co-sponsors.

t: ICE buys integration software for its STELLA AI platform and claims 12 deployed AI applications
d: From the archive (Oct 6, 2026): DHS's July AI inventory still listed the platform's assistant as pre-deployment, Biometric Update notes.

t: Two California county probation departments have agreements with the same AI vendor, each with a ceiling above $3 million
d: From the archive (Oct 6, 2026): Fresno County's agreement with Cognisen runs up to $3,085,149; San Mateo County added a conversational AI assistant in September. Both county records say staff review what the software drafts.

t: A Santa Clara County judge dismisses a state-constitution challenge to San Jose's network of more than 500 plate readers
d: From the archive (Oct 6, 2026): The ACLU and EFF had argued warrantless police searches of the data violate the California Constitution.

t: Milford, Michigan, votes 7-0 to remove its remaining Flock plate-reader cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 5, 2026): The police chief cited problems with the vendor, not the cameras' effectiveness.

t: A DuPage County grand jury indicts two former suburban Chicago officers over alleged misuse of Flock plate-reader searches
d: From the archive (Oct 5, 2026): One former Itasca officer faces 13 felony official misconduct counts; the charges are allegations.

t: San Francisco car crime has plunged. NPR asks how much credit Flock cameras deserve
d: From the archive (Oct 2, 2026): The one study cited found an 11% drop in car thefts across 216 agencies; it isn't peer-reviewed and didn't examine break-ins.

t: Oregon lawmakers from both parties plan a 2027 push to ban Flock and other plate-reader cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 2, 2026): A 2026 law already caps police retention of plate-reader data at 30 days.

t: Davie County sheriff tells commissioners plate-reader searches are now audited every 30 days
d: From the archive (Oct 1, 2026): Audits used to happen every 90 days; each search now needs a reason and a case number, the sheriff said.

t: UMass study offers cities a way to weigh surveillance tech like Flock cameras
d: From the archive (Oct 1, 2026): The research proposes "public value mapping" and examines facial recognition in Portland, Oregon.

t: San José coalition demands an end to Flock cameras after an officer misused plate-reader data
d: From the archive (Oct 1, 2026): The officer was fired after a yearlong investigation; the city runs 474 cameras.

t: Arizona appeals court orders a new sentencing hearing because a judge relied on an AI-generated video of the victim
d: From the archive (Oct 1, 2026): The panel upheld the manslaughter conviction but found the video prejudiced the sentence.

t: The ACLU sues San Diego and its police department to end use of Flock license plate readers
d: From the archive (Sep 30, 2026): The suit argues the city's plate readers violate Article 1 of the California constitution.

t: Apex, North Carolina, reconsiders its Flock plate-reader pilot after public-records findings
d: From the archive (Sep 29, 2026): Two federal agencies had access to the town's data as of March, according to records cited by INDY Week.

t: Tennessee prisons open an intelligence center using AI cameras, drones and counter-drone alerts against contraband
d: From the archive (Sep 29, 2026): The department says its drones logged more than 5,000 flights over the past year.

t: British Transport Police's six-month facial recognition trial at London stations produced one alert, a false match, then was extended
d: From the archive (Sep 29, 2026): Records obtained by Liberty Investigates show the trial cost £320,786 across 18 deployments.

t: ICE awards Thomson Reuters a data and analytics deal worth up to $125 million after one bidder responded
d: From the archive (Sep 28, 2026): ICE had planned a sole-source award, then opened the work to competition.

t: Winter Park, Florida, switches off its Flock and other plate-reader cameras for at least 90 days
d: From the archive (Sep 28, 2026): The police chief says a new policy may not be ready until early 2027.

t: Dutchess County's district attorney and sheriff move to phase out 64 Flock-style cameras as Poughkeepsie's mayor objects
d: From the archive (Sep 27, 2026): The county legislature's majority also planned a vote to end the cameras' use.

t: California budgets $2.2 million to add AI to its prison health records
d: From the archive (Sep 26, 2026): Funding is scheduled to rise to $4.5 million a year by 2028-29, with quarterly progress reports required.

t: UK justice ministry: AI note-taking reaches 12,000 probation officers, and predictive tools are live in prisons and probation
d: From the archive (Sep 24, 2026): The Ministry of Justice's one-year update to its AI Action Plan names a prison violence estimator, GPS crime mapping for people on probation, and facial recognition check-ins.

t: ICE plans a contract of more than $100 million to staff about 142 intelligence analysts across its enforcement operation
d: From the archive (Sep 24, 2026): A Sept. 18 request for information covers ERO headquarters, all 24 field areas and three targeting centers.

t: A Florida woman wrongly jailed for 13 days in a fatal-crash case testifies at a Senate hearing on Flock's AI camera network
d: From the archive (Sep 23, 2026): Charges were dropped after troopers found no crash damage on her car; the report does not say what led to her arrest.

t: Western Australia police report 79 arrests from a live facial recognition trial that scanned 905,117 faces
d: From the archive (Sep 22, 2026): Every false match in the trial misidentified a person with darker skin, the report says. Police say an officer confirms each match.

t: Cuyahoga County extends AI monitoring of jail phone calls to 2028
d: From the archive (Sep 22, 2026): The council added up to $2,695,757.68 for LEO Technologies' Verus software, paid from the Commissary Fund.

t: Justice Department asks vendors about AI legal assistants for a possible pilot
d: From the archive (Sep 21, 2026): The market research notice describes 20 to 30 users and no contract award.

t: U.S. jails expand round-the-clock biometric monitoring of people in custody as data rules lag
d: From the archive (Sep 21, 2026): A vendor says 80+ agencies use its wearables; one county keeps the data indefinitely and Ohio jails can require the devices.

t: Atlanta's mayor proposes monthly audits and new limits on police use of Flock plate readers and cameras
d: From the archive (Sep 20, 2026): A police audit found less than 1% of uses potentially improper, with nearly 80 cases flagged.

t: Tasmania reviews past parole decisions after a court voids a condition based on an AI-assisted document that cited non-existent case law
d: From the archive (Sep 19, 2026): The Supreme Court of Tasmania struck down a parole condition on Susan Neill-Fraser. The justice department then opened a review of AI use in past Parole Board decisions.

t: Federal judiciary's AI task force aims to release final guidance by year's end
d: From the archive (Sep 18, 2026): The group formed after two federal judges said AI use by staff led to error-riddled opinions.

t: National task force shows agencies how to decide on AI for police reports, public defense and prison classification
d: From the archive (Sep 16, 2026): The Council on Criminal Justice's AI task force applied its decision framework to three real-world tool categories.

t: Two House members, one from each party, introduce the No FLOCK Act to limit license plate readers through federal highway funding
d: From the archive (Sep 15, 2026): States without limits on plate readers would lose 10 percent of some federal transportation money under the bill.

t: Singapore Prison Service trials PROTECT, a patrol robot officers can use to deploy irritant spray remotely
d: From the archive (Sep 3, 2026): The robot uses AI-enabled navigation and streams live video and audio to a control centre.

t: Dutch police halt their nationwide predictive policing system after a decade
d: From the archive (Aug 18, 2026): An internal report found the Crime Anticipation System correctly predicted one of 50 Amsterdam incidents.

t: DHS has committed more than $2.9 billion to surveillance and data tools, Brennan Center finds
d: From the archive (Jul 29, 2026): Biometrics leads with more than $1 billion; commitments to Palantir rose from $20.4 million in 2024 to $162.2 million in 2026.

t: EFF: records show Sparks, Nevada, police plate readers use ICE's immigration hotlist, though the department lists immigration enforcement as a prohibited use
d: From the archive (Jun 25, 2026): Of 13 agencies that answered records requests, two had the hotlist enabled.

t: New York bill would bar the prison and parole department from using AI in parole release and supervision decisions
d: From the archive (May 14, 2026): Senate bill S10349, still in committee, names COMPAS as the system it targets.

t: Berkeley Law clinic warns that AI-enabled parole and probation monitors are used to send people back to prison with little scrutiny
d: From the archive (Feb 17, 2026): A Samuelson Clinic white paper calls for procedural reforms and limits on incarceration for technical violations.

t: Justice Department's AI inventory lists 315 uses, including a prison misconduct predictor
d: From the archive (Feb 11, 2026): The 2025 inventory, up 31% from the year before, flags 114 uses as high-impact.
